(CNN) -- Flamboyant and fearless, Roberto Cavalli is the peacock of the fashion world; with his body-hugging clothes, he woos women the world over. Fashion designer Roberto Cavalli . But his clients are no dainty damsels: Cavalli's women are Amazonian warriors and Grecian goddesses, whose armor is fashion and whose weapon is sex. His colorful creations are unabashed celebrations of the female form: dresses slashed to the hip or barely skimming the buttocks, necklines that plunge where no other designer dares. Cavalli's woman knows she looks fabulous, and isn't afraid to show it: to her, it's not just clothing, it's an announcement that she's arrived. Born in Florence in 1940, Cavalli was immersed in an intensely creative environment from childhood. That influence came from his father, a tailor, and his artist grandfather, Giuseppe Rossi, whose work is shown in the famous Uffizi Galleries. Following in his father's footsteps, Cavalli studied textile design at the local art institute. By the early 70s, he had developed an innovative technique for printing on lightweight leather, and his Florentine flair had led to commissions with Hermes and Pierre Cardin. In 1970, he presented his first namesake collection at the Salon for Prêt-à-Porter in Paris. His trademark work with unconventional fabrics like embellished denim and leather, mixed with wild animal prints and exotic patterns, was embraced by the jet set and Cavalli opened his first boutique in Saint Tropez in 1972. Cavalli married his wife, Eva Duringer, a former Miss Universe, in 1980; she is now his business partner and right-hand woman. His fondness for bright color, exotics, fur and bold prints -- which he designs in his factory on the outskirts of Florence -- have won him a name as the king of fashion excess. Beloved by A-listers and pop princesses, these are not clothes for the shy: this is old-school glamour, infused with power, wielded by women who have flounced and shimmied their way to the top.  See Cavalli's designs on the catwalk » . His main line is sold in over 50 countries worldwide, along with his diffusion lines RC Menswear and Just Cavalli, plus a children's line, knitwear, accessories, eyewear, watches, perfumes, underwear and beachwear. He's even ventured into Cavalli-branded vodka and wine. His collaboration with high-street fashion store H&M in November 2007 caused stampedes as his fans flocked to get their hands on his creations, desperate to capture some of that Cavalli magic at tiny prices. Some have asked whether his latest collections have taken a more gentle direction -- but the tiger's inner fire still burns bright. Spring/Summer 2008's bold flower prints and flirty feathered dresses were followed by Autumn/Winter 2008's flowered dresses that at first glance appear dewy and fresh -- but look closer, and the hip-hugging cut belies their innocence. Cavalli is adored by his celebrity clientele, who flaunt his show-stopping creations on red carpets from Los Angeles to Sydney. Fans of his work include Halle Berry, Sharon Stone, Madonna, Jennifer Lopez, Gwyneth Paltrow, Beyoncè Knowles, Charlize Theron and Victoria Beckham. If anyone sums up the glamour and glitz of show business, it's Cavalli: fashion as theatre, shameless decadence where the whole world is a stage. That's underlined by his eponymous 133'9" long yacht, built 2004, and color-coordinated, naturally, with his helicopter and fleet of cars.

# The Wild Heart of Fashion: Roberto Cavalli

*The Italian maestro who turned animal prints into high art and dressed a generation of stars in unapologetic glamour*

---

There are designers who whisper, and there are designers who roar. Roberto Cavalli belonged emphatically to the latter camp. For more than four decades, the Florentine visionary built an empire on the belief that fashion should be sensual, exuberant, and utterly fearless—a philosophy that made him one of the most recognizable names in luxury and a favorite among the world's most glamorous women.

## Tuscan Roots

Born in Florence in 1940, Roberto Cavalli was, in many ways, destined for a life in the arts. His grandfather, Giuseppe Rossi, was a painter associated with the Macchiaioli movement, whose works hang in the prestigious Uffizi Gallery. That artistic bloodline coursed through Cavalli's veins and shaped his approach to design—he always considered himself a painter first, one who simply chose fabric as his canvas.

He studied at the Academy of Art in Florence, where he first began experimenting with textile printing. It was this technical foundation—an obsession with color, pattern, and the alchemy of print—that would define his entire career.

## Building an Empire

Cavalli's breakthrough came in the early 1970s when he invented and patented a revolutionary printing process on leather. The innovation caught the attention of major fashion houses, and by 1972 he was showing his own collection at the Salon for Prêt-à-Porter in Paris. His debut at the Palazzo Pitti in Florence soon followed, launching him into the international spotlight.

The decades that followed brought signature innovations: sandblasted denim, patchwork designs, and printed materials that no one else dared to attempt. But it was the 1990s and 2000s that cemented his legend. As fashion embraced maximalism and celebrity culture exploded, Cavalli's over-the-top glamour found its perfect moment.

## The Signature Look

To wear Cavalli was to make a statement. His aesthetic was instantly identifiable: bold animal prints—leopard, zebra, snakeskin—rendered in vivid, saturated color. There were figure-hugging silhouettes, plunging necklines, feathers, sequins, and an unabashed celebration of the female form.

"I love women, and I want to make them feel sexy and confident," Cavalli often said, and his designs delivered exactly that. His style was rock-and-roll opulence, Baroque excess filtered through a distinctly Italian sensibility. He wasn't interested in minimalism or restraint; he wanted drama, romance, and a touch of the untamed.

His lifestyle matched his aesthetic. Cavalli was famous for his flamboyant persona—the flowing hair, the yacht, the Tuscan estate, the collection of exotic animals, and a love of the good life that made him as colorful a character as his creations.

## The Celebrity Following

If any designer understood the symbiotic relationship between fashion and fame, it was Cavalli. His designs became red-carpet staples and paparazzi magnets, worn by a constellation of A-list stars.

Jennifer Lopez, Beyoncé, Cindy Crawford, Naomi Campbell, and Aishwarya Rai all embraced his glamorous vision. He created custom looks for Shakira, Jennifer Aniston, and Victoria Beckham. When pop stars wanted to command attention on stage or on the carpet, Cavalli was frequently the name they called.

His influence extended into music, too—he collaborated on tour wardrobes and became a fixture in celebrity circles, his parties legendary for their star-studded guest lists. The Cavalli brand expanded into fragrances, accessories, eyewear, and even a vodka line and nightclubs, transforming a fashion label into a full-fledged lifestyle empire.

## A Lasting Legacy

Roberto Cavalli stepped back from his namesake company in 2015, and he passed away in April 2024 at the age of 83. But his imprint on fashion endures. He proved that Italian design could be as wild as it was refined, that prints could be as powerful as any silhouette, and that glamour—real, unapologetic glamour—never truly goes out of style.

In an industry that often prizes cool detachment, Cavalli offered heat, color, and life. He was, until the end, fashion's great romantic—a man who dressed women not to blend in, but to be impossible to ignore.

For more than five decades, Roberto Cavalli built a fashion empire on a single, audacious philosophy: more is more. His aesthetic was never subtle—and that was precisely the point.

Born in Florence in 1940, Cavalli grew up surrounded by artistry. His grandfather, Giuseppe Rossi, was a painter associated with the Macchiaioli movement, and that lineage of bold Italian visual expression would echo throughout Cavalli's career. He studied at the Academy of Art in Florence, where he first began experimenting with textile prints—a fascination that would become his signature.

In the late 1960s, Cavalli pioneered a printing technique on leather that would set him apart. This innovation opened doors quickly. By 1970, he was showing his creations in Paris, and soon fashion houses like Hermès and Pierre Cardin were taking notice of the young Italian's unconventional approach to materials.

If a single garment could define the Cavalli universe, it might be a slinky, body-hugging gown drenched in leopard print, glittering with embellishment, and cut to celebrate—never conceal—the female form.

- **Exotic animal prints** that became almost synonymous with his name
- **Sensual, form-fitting silhouettes** that embraced the body
- **Lavish embellishment**, from beading to feathers to gold
- **A bohemian rock-and-roll spirit** that channeled decadent glamour

Cavalli designed for women who wanted to be seen. His clothes were, in a sense, a rejection of minimalism's cool detachment—a full-throated celebration of sensuality, wildness, and joy.

## Dressing the Stars

By the 1990s and 2000s, Cavalli had become the go-to designer for a certain kind of red-carpet moment: the one that demanded attention. Celebrities including Jennifer Lopez, Beyoncé, Aisha Tyler, and countless others gravitated toward his glamorous, boundary-pushing designs.

His diffusion line, Just Cavalli, extended his vision to younger and more accessible markets, while his empire expanded to include everything from fragrances to home goods to a Miami nightclub. The Cavalli name became shorthand for a lifestyle—glamorous, indulgent, and utterly without apology.

Cavalli stepped away from his eponymous label in 2015, and the brand has since passed through new creative hands seeking to reinterpret his maximalist vision for contemporary audiences. He died in April 2024 at the age of 83, leaving behind a body of work that helped define an era of Italian fashion.

His influence endures in every designer who dares to embrace boldness over restraint, spectacle over subtlety. In an industry that often prizes cool detachment, Roberto Cavalli offered something warmer and wilder—a reminder that fashion, at its best, can be pure, uninhibited pleasure.

He didn't just make clothes. He made a statement: that glamour, however excessive, is always worth celebrating.

---

---
